overviews.title: The Job
overviews.body:
Session One: The Job

The party is hired by Horus Lanternholder, a Gatecrasher and planewalker, as guard for a quick delivery run to the seventh layer of Baator. He travels with his donkey, Toloin, who carries two bags of holding on either side. The left bag holds Horus's personal effects. The right bag is his trash. The delivery itself is clean. The trade is made. Nothing goes wrong.

On the way back to the portal, a group of powerful devils intercepts the party. They address Horus directly. He has a life debt. It is due now. It does not matter what the party does, what they roll, or how they intervene. Horus dies. The devils let the party go.

DESIGN NOTE

The death is scripted. Do not give the impression that the right roll could have saved him. The devils are not interested in the party at all.

Once back in Sigil the party will notice the two bags of holding on Toloin. Both are empty. What was in the delivery bag is never confirmed. That question can sit unanswered for a long time.

Three Visitors

The party returns to the hotel where they met Horus. Three visitors arrive separately.

The Lawyer
One-time NPC unless the party seeks his office later

Arrives with the contract Horus signed, explains the inheritance clause plainly, and hands over a key. The party now legally owns whatever Horus owned, including his debts. He does not editorialize. He hands over the paperwork and leaves.

Devin Quelch
Human Gatecrasher, first ioun stone claimant

He and Horus had a partnership agreement: they would share ownership of an ioun stone Horus was tracking down. Horus has been stalling him for months. He arrives with muscle because he can afford it, not because he could use it himself. He does not know what the ioun stone actually does. He just knows it is valuable and he has a claim.

He gives the party the same line the BBEG will give them later: he will be back after they have had time to look around. Coming from Quelch it sounds like bluster.

[CASK CAPO NAME]
Cask Family capo, debt collector

Arrives with bruisers but is not here to threaten. He is here to introduce himself and make it clear that the debt is not forgiven by death. Horus owed 2,500 gp in protection money. The house changed hands. The debt did not. He is polite, direct, and unbothered. He has done this before.

Finding the House

The party has a key but no address. A stable runner finds them to let them know Toloin is still stabled and waiting. That is their first practical help.

Encounter

They find the house in the Hive, near the ward border. When they arrive, three Rusted Bell members are mid-robbery: a bruiser, a skirmisher, and an instigator. They found nothing worth taking. They are trashing it on principle because it belongs to outsiders. Pure combat.

Exploring the House

No investigation check walls. They find things because they are looking.

A rug in the kitchen covers a trapdoor. Below it are crates. A good number of the items are magical. The Umbrulla is in here: it just expands to cover more people. The bag of withholding is among the crates. It will not open for anyone. Only its creator can open it.

1Prose and Poetry of Jaden Abora
2Pet Rock
3Otik's Frying Pan
4Elemental Bolt Pouch
5Silvia's Self Cleaning Sauce Pan
6Portal to New Haven
7Bag of Colding
8Bag of Olding
9Bag of Withholding
10Djinn Jars
11Everlight Lantern
12Flame Flicker Torch
13Zorin's Umbrulla
14Deck of 42 Slices
15Mudd's Stone
16The Vesll
17Crass' Wind Bag
18Campfire Cord
19Pocket of Maybe Useful Items
20Ring of Protection
21Shattersmith
22The Mysteries of the Deep Ethereal
23History of Korvash
24Angels and Demons Clash, a Romance
25Jawclasp on the High Seas, a Romance
26Contracts (file cabinet upstairs)
27Delivery contract record for New Haven

The two bags of holding are still on Toloin at the stables. The party will need to return to the donkey to deal with them. The left bag holds Horus's personal effects. The right bag holds viscera and garbage from the delivery. To find out what is inside they have to dump them.

LEFT BAG — PERSONAL EFFECTS
  • 25 soul pyramids (75 gp)
  • Short sword and shield
  • Bottle of good wine
  • Dwarven stein (glass bottom)
  • 5 field rations
  • Bedroll
  • 10 torches
  • Wood axe
  • Costume pearl necklace
  • Regular healing potion
  • ★ Child's drawing — keep this. It matters.

When the party exits the house, a man is sitting across the road doing contact juggling with a glowing ioun stone. He does not need to describe what he wants. He just shows them. He has the same story as Devin Quelch — Horus promised him a share. He has been patient. He is done being patient. He is not Quelch. He is calm where Quelch was pushy. His muscle is real where Quelch's was cosmetic. He mentions helpfully that there appear to be corpses in their house and that the Dabus and Harmonium will not look kindly on that. Then he leaves.

NOTE

This man is Grey Reed. He does not reveal this. The ioun stone he is juggling is the one he already owns. The confidence is real. He watched Horus dump the bags. He knows exactly which crate stone 2 is sitting in.

The party will need to deal with the Rusted Bell corpses. They will eventually find the Mortuary and the Dustmen. After that they take a few days to settle in: get a mimir attuned, sort through the loot, learn which streets to avoid, and start getting their bearings. Arc 1 begins here.

overviews.title: The Hive
overviews.body:
The party arrives in Sigil deep in debt: 2,500 gp owed to two rival criminal families, the Casks and the Ninefold. They take jobs from both sides to stay alive and pay down what they owe, while a third party, the Gray Ledger, quietly profits from the conflict.

The bag of withholding (ioun stone 2 hidden inside) is already in party hands. The war architect behind the Ledger is the campaign's BBEG: Grey Reed.

The Cask Family

Old-guard protection racket. Led by Mother Veshka Cask, a tiefling matriarch. Her rule: nobody sleeps safe in the Hive without paying. The debt is about precedent, not money.

The Ninefold

Upstart planewalkers who control a stable portal in a collapsed tenement. Led by "Salt" Orrin Tamb. He borrowed heavily from the Xaositects to secure the portal. When that deadline hits, the Chaosmen take it.

The Gray Ledger

A quiet independent broker who lends to both families and profits from escalation. It staged the killing that started the war. The party will not learn this until the arc resolves.

The Rusted Bell

About a dozen Hive-born bashers led by Tannit Brask, a half-orc ex-Cask enforcer. They hate outsiders. They work both sides for pay, which means information about the party flows to both families through them.

The Tension Track

0
1
2
3
4
5
6
0Business as usual. Jobs available from both sides. No eyes on the party yet.
1The party is noticed. Runners from both sides watch them. One stall owner refuses to deal with them.
2A body turns up in an alley tied to a recent job. Both sides watch openly now.
3A note under the door, or a scuffle. Each side hints the other is responsible.
4The tenement fire. Dabus appear on nearby rooftops but do not intervene.
5Open street fighting. Shops shutter. Harmonium doubles patrols. Both factions blame the party.
6The gang war. The Gray Ledger calls in both debts at once. See below.
RULE

Each Cask or Ninefold job raises Tension by 1. Working both sides raises it faster.

The Payoff Rule

After any faction job, the party can pay part of the reward to the other faction and cancel that job's +1 Tension. Cost scales with current Tension:

Tension 0–3One third of the reward
Tension 4–5One half of the reward
Tension 6Payoff no longer works

Cask rewards are debt credit, so Ninefold payoffs come out of pocket.

OPEN QUESTION

Does Ninefold jink paid to the Casks count toward the 2,500 gp debt?

Tension 6: The Gang War

The Gray Ledger calls in both debts simultaneously. Three gangs converge in the street: Casks, Ninefold, and the Rusted Bell. The party hears about it as a cut scene and does not play it out.

The Lady of Pain mazes three people mid-fight, with no warning and no combat: each one simply stops existing between one breath and the next.

  • The Cask second in command (the same person from Beat 1)
  • The Ninefold second in command (name TBD)
  • Tannit Brask, Rusted Bell leader

Veshka Cask and Salt Orrin Tamb survive, both cut down in power. The Xaositects take the Ninefold portal. The Gray Ledger wins technically. The Dustmen and Xaositects win by not being involved.

NEW REVENGE THREAD

The Rusted Bell's second in command takes over from Tannit and blames the party for the mazing. The party receives a letter. Name and letter text still to write.

Beat Sequence

Beat 1: The Chair

The party comes home to find someone already inside. [CASK LIEUTENANT NAME] and a few bruisers. Nothing is damaged. Nothing is taken. He is sitting in a chair. This is the reminder that protection money is not optional and a demonstration of exactly what it buys. He restates the debt calmly and leaves.

Beat 2: S.I.G.I.S. Jobs

Two ads in the newsletter give the party work while the Hive arc develops. Income and breathing room between mafia beats. See the S.I.G.I.S. Ad Pool for full details: Stolen Necklace (Foundry Ward recovery, seeds a larger criminal operation) and Sewer Monster (seeds the sewer location for the Torvin Baale module).

Beat 3: The Street Robbery

Two Rusted Bell members steal a purse from a party member and split up immediately: one down the road, one down the alley. Each fight is one Bell member against two PCs, with slightly boosted HP. Whichever runner the party reaches first dies or is subdued. The other escapes to Tannit Brask. The party is now confirmed enemies of the Rusted Bell.

Maps: Road (Beat 3 road runner) and Alley (Beat 3 alley runner) are both built. Both maps double for faction jobs.

Beat 4: The Ninefold Approach

A Ninefold-affiliated contact watched the street encounter and approaches the party afterward. They do not identify themselves or their employer. They say only that the party seems capable and that rising tensions in the ward mean there is work available for the right people.

Beat 5: The Cask Offer

[CASK CAPO NAME] returns. This time with an offer: the party can work off the 2,500 gp debt through Cask jobs. Each job knocks off 250 to 500 gp. It is at this point the party may realize the earlier approach did not come from these people.

FACTION JOBS

The Hive War Quest

Arc Resolution

The Gray Ledger staged the bagman killing that started the war. Three converging clues establish this. The party does not need all three: any two are enough to act on. All three make the confrontation airtight.

Clue 1: The Portal Key

This clue enters play when the party first encounters the dead bagman, the killing that started everything. The body has already been found by the time the party arrives in the Hive. It is a street fact: everyone knows a Ninefold courier was killed on Cask turf with a Cask knife left in him. The Casks say they did not send anyone. The Ninefold say the knife was one of theirs, stolen.

The body is at the Mortuary now. The party can get to it one of two ways: through a contact who works the cremation shift, or by doing a favor for the Dustmen. Either way, examining the body before it burns is a one-shot window.

WHAT THE BODY HOLDS

The knife is real Cask work: the party can confirm this. But the bagman also has a portal key wedged in his mouth, under the tongue, where a killer in a hurry would not think to look. The key has a specific glyph sequence. Investigation DC 13 or a Ninefold contact identifies it: this key was cut for a portal the Ninefold sealed and abandoned months ago after a bad run. No current member carries one. Someone dug this out of old inventory. Someone who knew enough about the Ninefold's dead portals to know where the key would have been stored.

DM NOTE

This clue alone does not name anyone. It rules out a current Ninefold member as the killer and establishes that whoever did this had deep knowledge of Ninefold operations. The party should sit with that for a session before the next clue lands.

Clue 2: The Rat's Receipt

This clue comes through the Cask job Find the Rat. Veshka wants to know who has been leaking Cask movement schedules to the Ninefold. The party tracks it down.

The rat is a Cask-adjacent street vendor, a spice merchant two blocks from the Cask counting house. He has been passing scraps: delivery routes, rough timing. Not because he believes in the Ninefold. He is in debt. He borrowed from a moneylender eight months ago to cover a bad shipment. He has been paying it back in information because he cannot pay it back in coin.

PLAYING THE SCENE

He does not run when cornered. He is scared but not stupid. If the party gives him room to talk before turning him in, he tells all of it: the loan, the moneylender, what he passed, how often. He knows he is finished. He asks only that his sister not be told how he went out. Then he produces the receipt: the original loan document he has been keeping because he thought he might need it. It is stamped with a mark he cannot read. He has seen it on a shop front near the Mortuary gate. He has paid it no attention. It is just a mark on paper to him.

If the party turns him in to Veshka without hearing him out, the receipt goes with him and they lose this thread. Veshka will not offer it back. She considers it fair payment for the job.

If the party delivers the rat and holds onto the receipt (or takes it first), they have the address. They also get the Cask reward and a small complication: Veshka knows they talked to him at length. She does not know what he told them. She will notice if they start following up on a moneylender she has never heard of.

Clue 3: The Books

The receipt leads to a shop front near the Mortuary gate: a legitimate ground-floor merchant selling lamp oil, candles, and sundry goods. Unremarkable. The sign above the door has a small stamped mark that matches the receipt, a ledger page with a single line through it. The party has probably walked past it a dozen times.

Getting into the back room requires infiltration. The shop has two employees visible during the day, a locked counting room in back, and a second entrance through a courtyard shared with a tallow renderer next door. The books are in the counting room.

THE SHOP FRONT — APPROACHES

Stealth: The courtyard entrance is a DC 14 lock. The counting room is DC 16. One employee takes a meal break at the Mortuary gate food stall every midday: reliable enough to plan around.

Social: The front employee (a young tiefling named Wex, earnest, completely in the dark about the back room) can be distracted or sent on an errand. The back-room clerk, Drusine, is harder: she is the one who keeps the books and she does not leave the counting room during business hours.

Direct: Drusine will not talk. She knows who she works for. If cornered she stalls, she deflects, she calls for help. She does not break. She is not paid enough to die for it but she is paid enough not to break under a Persuasion check.

The books show loans to both the Cask Family and the Ninefold under their operating names: not personal names, but business names the party can verify with either faction. Same ledger. Same hand. Active accounts. The most recent entry on the Cask side is dated three days before the bagman was killed.

WHAT THE BOOKS PROVE

Nobody lends to both sides of a war unless they own the war. The party cannot yet prove the Gray Ledger killed the bagman: but they can prove that the Gray Ledger was financing both families simultaneously and had current access to Cask operations through the rat. The inference is not a leap. The portal key makes it less of one. Two clues and the books together close it.

The Confrontation

Once the party has at least two clues, they can bring this to either or both leaders. This is not a combat scene. It is a negotiation, and the party's leverage depends on what they are holding and how they play it.

Going to Veshka alone

She listens without moving. She asks three questions: how did you find this, who else knows, and what do you want. She has already been thinking the war does not add up. This confirms it. She will agree to a ceasefire if the party can deliver the same evidence to Salt. She will not go to him herself. She does not trust him not to use the meeting as cover for a strike.

Going to Salt alone

He is relieved in a way that makes him seem younger than he is. He already suspected he was being played: the Xaositect pressure on the portal happened right after the killing, too fast to be coincidence. He will agree to a ceasefire if the party brings Veshka the same offer. He will not approach her. He does not believe she would hear him without a weapon in her hand.

Going to both at once

This requires setting the meeting, which requires both leaders to agree to a location neither controls. The Mortuary neutral ground works: the Dustmen allow it as a matter of policy, death being the great equalizer. The scene is tense. Veshka and Salt do not speak to each other directly for the first half of the meeting. The party is the medium. When the evidence lands on the table both of them go quiet in a way that is more frightening than shouting. Then Veshka says: "The Ledger owns this street. Or it thought it did." That is the end of the war.

GRAY LEDGER STATUS AFTER THE REVEAL

The operation is exposed, not destroyed. The shop front will be cleared out within a day of the meeting: Drusine is not there the next morning, the counting room is empty, the books are gone. The Casks and Ninefold each have debts to the Ledger that are now in dispute. The party knows the symbol. They do not know who runs it, how large it is, or what it was building toward. That is a thread for later.

Endings and Payouts

Expose the Gray Ledger / broker the ceasefire

Veshka clears the 2,500 gp debt entirely. Salt gives the party a cut of one portal cycle (400 gp) and a standing invitation to use the tenement portal at no charge. Tension resets. Both leaders owe the party a favor. The Gray Ledger goes quiet, not gone.

Expose the Gray Ledger to one family only

That family clears the debt or pays the reward. The other family hears about it eventually and is suspicious: why did the party bring this to their enemy first? Mild long-term friction.

Side fully with one family

The other becomes a long-term enemy. The war ends through attrition or dominance, not revelation. The Gray Ledger is never exposed and files the party's names under "useful leverage."

Ignore the war and hit Tension 6

The Gang War cut scene fires. See the Tension Track section.

Ignore the war entirely

Scrape 2,500 gp through jobs or independent means. Leave the Hive with no faction ties, no enemies, and no allies. The Gray Ledger has no particular interest in the party but notes them as competent and unattached: the kind of people worth watching.

overviews.title: Week of Indulgence
overviews.body:
A citywide festival follows the Hive arc. A full break before the next act. The party has breathing room, Sigil is loud and celebratory, and nothing is on fire for once.

  • Multiple games in the parks (what few there are)
  • Fireworks in the ring
  • Guildhall is hosting recruitment from the 13 factions
  • A parade
  • Coupons and deals from inns and taverns
  • Speeches from planeswalkers
  • Concerts in the Hall of Speakers
  • A collectable card game tournament

Shemeshka's Casino: The Free Spin

ARC 2 STARTS HERE

The moment the party walks through the casino doors, Arc 2 begins. The Hive arc was one ward, two families, known streets. From here Sigil opens up: new districts, new factions, new scale. The world gets bigger.

The festival includes a complimentary spin at Shemeshka's casino, distributed as a festival token. It feels like a gift from the city. The party collects it and Shemeshka is there. She has been waiting. She lets them come to her.

She has heard they inherited Horus's house. She expresses interest in the bag: not aggressively, just enough to let them know she knows. The party has already seen what everyone who wanted Horus's things was after, so their guard goes up. They won't give her anything. She does not press. She plants the question instead and lets it sit.

Before they leave she offers a contact. "You're still a little clueless in this new environment. I have a friend." She gives them a blank piece of paper with her seal and tells them to deliver it. No explanation of what it says. Because it says nothing. The seal is the message.

WHAT THE SEAL MEANS

The hag receives the paper, sees the seal, and takes the meeting. She does not need to know why. Shemeshka asked. The real intent: I need them busy. The party will not know this. They will think Shemeshka was being generous. She was moving a piece.

The hag turns out to be genuinely useful: she knows Sigil, she answers questions, she points them toward the market or the library when they are lost. Before they leave her shop she has a job for them. No second meeting. One visit: resource, then obligation. They walk out having gained a contact and taken on a heist (Heist of the Red Sensation Museum) without fully deciding to. Shemeshka's note said to complicate them. The hag delivered on the first meeting.

BACKUP

If the casino visit does not land naturally, Shemeshka sends a summons instead. She has heard about the bag regardless.

The Wandering Flame Parade

The Wandering Flame marches in the parade. This is the party's first clear look at the guild as an institution: banners, formation, presence. Horus's contracts in the file cabinet are their existing connection. The Week of Indulgence is when membership becomes a real option — the Guildhall opens recruitment during the festival. After the parade ends and the festival closes, the party can go to the guild hall and pursue it properly.

REFERENCE

March of the Wandering Flame — parade visual reference

Concert from the Bard of Five

Formerly a group of Horus's, these adventurers found more enjoyment — and coin — in singing and spreading joy than bringing pain for contracts. They perform during the Week of Indulgence.

REFERENCE

One More Round — concert vibe reference

The Wandering Flame

A small adventuring party that grew into a cross-planar guild. Members pool funds, share equipment, and take assigned contracts. Proceeds are turned in; a fraction is paid back to the completing party. They take care of you, but they get a good cut.

Horus did not found it. He found the founders when they were still clueless and helped them get their footing. Once they did not need him anymore they built the guild. He is their origin story. His death lands hard.

Membership Trial

The party goes to the guild hall after the Week of Indulgence. The founders are there. Good reunion energy, good laughs about Horus, then the sadness. Then how it works.

A lieutenant is in charge of new member admissions. He is high-ranking, protective, and skeptical. Normal admittance parties get a standard job. The party gets a hard one: missing children taken by a forest spirit in the Outlands.

Road Encounter: Pandemonium Merchant

A few days on the road between the portal drop and the township. One encounter on the way: a tiny merchant cart from Pandemonium. Just him and his goods and his very normal attitude about all of it.

Pandemonium Stone Earplugs (pair)

Carved from the tunnel walls, dense and oddly warm. They actually work.

Sideways Lantern

Burns at a 45-degree angle no matter how you hold it. Light still reaches the floor, just wrong.

Screaming Apples

Small, red, nutritious. They make a faint whine when bitten. Otherwise normal fruit.

Untangling Rope (50 ft)

Always tries to straighten itself out. Never knots on its own. Mildly annoying.

Wind-Dried Jerky

Cured in the tunnels. Unusual flavor. Keeps indefinitely. The merchant is very proud of it.

Pandemonium Pitons (6)

Iron spikes that vibrate faintly in your hand. Drive true. Hold well.

The Still Mirror ★ Prize Item

A hand mirror, roughly 8 inches across. Every surface in Pandemonium distorts. This one does not. It shows exactly what is in front of it: no noise, no movement in the reflection, perfectly silent. In Pandemonium that made it sacred. Out here it is just a very good mirror. Except sometimes, not often, the reflection is a half-second behind.

The Forest Spirit Quest

The Township

Small and frightened in a quiet way: the kind of frightened that has been going on long enough to become normal.

The Parents
Contract filers

Give the party the facts plainly. Children went into the forest a tenday ago following lights. None came back. Adults who followed heard music and laughter and came back wrong, dazed and disoriented. Nobody will go near the tree line anymore.

The Village Elder
Practical, not panicked

He has a township to run. He answers questions, offers a place to sleep, and is quietly relieved someone else is handling this. He has already mentally filed it as above his authority.

The Nurse
Sick house, near the tree line

Has been watching the forest from that window for years. Not afraid of the spirit. Listened while a patient talked in their sleep after following the children into the forest for a week.

WHAT THE NURSE KNOWS

The spirit does not take, it invites. It does not understand time or the concept of home as somewhere you miss. Fire is the wrong move. The way to reach it is through the children. Get to them and the spirit will come to you.

HERB TASK

The nurse trades for herbs that grow at the forest edge. Nobody goes near the tree line anymore. Supplies are running low. Not a quest. A task that puts the party at the tree line with their eyes open. Reward: a healing potion scaled to level, delivered over several turns instead of all at once. Smells like the forest and something baked.

The Forest

At the tree line: normal. The forest does not announce itself as dangerous. The edge is just an edge.

GATHERING THE HERBS

The moment they start pulling live plants the forest notices. Birds go quiet. The canopy thickens slightly. Nothing is threatening them. The forest is paying attention. If they stop and put the herbs down, the light comes back a little.

A cutting tool and a pot to transfer a live plant rather than pulling it up: the forest never reacts at all. Nobody has tried this in a long time.

The first sound: A child's giggle, from the left. Then a few seconds later from the right, slightly different child, same game. It is not sinister. It is delighted, mid-game. The party is not being lured. They are being included.

The music: A recorder. Badly played. Three notes, very committed, slightly wrong tempo, one note that always comes in a beat late. Then a second recorder joins. Different three notes. No coordination. Both completely confident.

The Thorn Wall

Spans the path completely, fifteen feet high, too dense to see through. Two thorn protectors stand at the base, one on each side: animated thorns, vaguely humanoid, no faces, bows of twisted branch that fire hardened thorn bolts. Still until the party gets close. They do not pursue past the wall.

STAT BLOCK

Initiative map and stat block are open items. Two archer-type animated thorn constructs, stationary, do not pursue past the wall, roots create difficult terrain, Dex saves for fast movement.

The wall does not open after the fight. Hacking through it works, but the forest reacts. The nurse's knowledge pays off here: leave something at the base — food, a small object, something living — and the wall opens a passage wide enough to walk through single file.

After the thorn wall: All movement is difficult terrain. Every foot costs two. Double movement requires a DC 13 Dexterity saving throw or go prone. No damage, just prone. The children move through it like it is not there.

The Clearing

The largest oak in the clearing is the spirit. The party may not realize this at first. It becomes apparent when a branch lowers slowly toward a crying child, the way you would crouch to a child's level. A cluster of small lights drifts from the canopy. The bark shifts into something that might be a face if you are looking for one.

The spirit communicates through the forest: warmth, light, the direction branches lean, whether the ground feels welcoming or firm underfoot. A druid or nature background feels this clearly. Everyone else gets impressions.

The Three Groups of Children
The Happy Ones

In the middle of the clearing, fully in the spirit's orbit. They see the party as new arrivals to the game, not rescuers.

The Hidden Ones

Tucked into roots and hollows at the tree line. Withdrawn, quiet. Easiest to reach. A calm voice, a familiar name, eye contact at their level.

The Scared Ones

Want to go home and know it but cannot find the edge of the forest. The spirit keeps bringing them things trying to fix something it cannot name. Closest to the spirit. Getting to them means getting close to it first.

Talking to the Spirit

The spirit does not process words as meaning. No Persuasion, Deception, Performance, or any Charisma roll. A bard monologuing at a tree is noise. Asking the DM for a Charisma roll is itself a heat tick, because the ask is the tell.

The spirit evaluates intent through action and object. Show it. Bring it evidence. Every action that demonstrates care builds trust. Every word erodes it.

The Collectible Card Hunt

Nine collectible cards are hidden across Sigil as a festival game. The game is introduced by the Voice of the Lady of Pain: a formal, citywide announcement, which is itself an event. The Lady does not speak. Something speaks for her. The cards are the game.

THE FULL SET: 27 CARDS

The festival game presents 9 cards as a children's scavenger hunt. The party will not learn until later that these are part of a set of 27. The set has escalating magical power: 9 cards unlocks something, 18 unlocks more, 27 is the full effect. The first 9 are hidden across Sigil's wards as part of the game. The remaining 18 are out in the planes, likely carried by merchants in the Outlands (integration TBD). The children who play this game have no idea what they are holding.

OPEN ITEMS

Card locations (Sigil 9), card content, the 18 Outlands cards and who carries them, and what each tier of 9/18/27 unlocks are all to be developed.

Kamal Dezpot

Geomancer — public speech, Week of Indulgence

Dezpot gives a public speech during the festival. Topics: planeswalking as discipline, spellslinging culture, and the process of bonding a gen. Covered as a story in S.I.G.I.S. (issue in progress, needs editing). Day within the week not yet assigned.

After the speech he sells two items from a small table.

Booklet (title TBD)

Requires an Intelligence check and one week of non-continuous study. On success, the reader qualifies to multiclass into Sha'ir.

Small jar

Contains an unbounded gen. Opening the jar requires a one-hour ritual performed after completing the study. The gen inside is very unruly.

overviews.title: The Withholding Research Arc
overviews.body:
The bag of withholding is strange. Researchers at Fortune's Wheel and leads from the Threadbare module point toward its origin and what it contains. The Red Sensation heist is a side quest that runs through this arc.

Ioun stone 2 is still inside the bag. The party is getting closer to understanding why.

overviews.title: Mock Modron March / Horus's Mail
overviews.body: Two short interludes bridge the gap between Arc 2 and Arc 3. The Mock Modron March is a Sigil spectacle. Horus's Mail is a courier job with a stranger payload than advertised. Both nudge the party toward the Beastlands.

overviews.title: Wyrd and Wyld
overviews.body: The Beastlands. A dryad with a secret. Nazir's journal turns up — the first fragment of a trail that will carry the campaign through four more arcs. The arc earns its name from the tension between wildness and fate.

overviews.title: Meet Nazir
overviews.body: The journal led here. Nazir is a Deep Ethereal navigator and the only person who can guide the party to where ioun stone 3 is hidden. This is the introduction: wary on both sides, but necessary.

overviews.title: Al-Qadim
overviews.body: One town. One city. Ioun stone 3 is inside the Sheridish Mirror. The arc's shape is still forming, but the destination is clear.

overviews.title: New Haven Gate Breaks
overviews.body: The New Haven gate into the demiplane fractures and goes dark. The demiplane still exists but has no way in. The party cannot reach ioun stone 4 without Nazir — he is the only one who can navigate the Deep Ethereal to find it. The party's dependence on him becomes explicit.

overviews.title: Frostmore
overviews.body: One large city. Nazir's Journal Part 4 is here — the next piece of the trail to ioun stone 4. The arc is shorter than the others. Its exact shape is still rough.

overviews.title: Nazir Taken
overviews.body: Nazir is pulled into the Ordial Plane off-screen. The party has no warning. He is unreachable: divination cannot find him, his usual contacts have nothing. His journal is now the only guide to ioun stone 4 — the navigator is gone and his notes have to do the work instead.

overviews.title: The Theft on the Plane of Fire
overviews.body: The party is banished to the Plane of Fire. While they are down, Grey Reed's minion lifts one ioun stone from the repacked bag. Entering Arc 6: Grey Reed holds two stones, the party holds one. Stone 4 is inside the demiplane. Whoever secures it sets the endgame balance.

overviews.title: The Demiplane Island
overviews.body: The demiplane the party has been locked out of since Transition 4. Complex, puzzle-heavy, long. Ioun stone 4 is here. The arc's full shape is still being built.

overviews.title: Rescue Nazir
overviews.body: Entry into the Ordial Plane requires three personal tests: one of pain, one of skill, one of belief. This is not students retrieving a mentor. Nazir and the party meet as peers, shaped by everything that came before. The reunion earns its weight.

overviews.title: The Pedestal
overviews.body: Two stones each. The pedestal requires all four to activate. Nobody can leave without the other side's stones. The standoff is the campaign's final scene: what the party does with that moment is the ending.

worldLore.title: The Great Wheel
worldLore.body:
The multiverse is a wheel. Sigil sits at the hub, floating atop the Spire in the Outlands. The Outlands ring the Spire. Sixteen Outer Planes ring the Outlands, arranged by alignment — law to the east, chaos to the west, good above, evil below. The Inner Planes ring everything: raw elemental matter, the stuff the Outer Planes are shaped from.

Rule one: belief shapes reality out here. The more cagers believe something, the more true it becomes. Rule two: each plane has a dominant tone — enter Mechanus and you want to organize things; enter the Abyss and you want to destroy them. Fight the tone or it fights you. Rule three: no portal, no exit. Know your key before you step through.

worldLore.title: The Outlands
worldLore.body:
The center of the Great Wheel. Neutral ground — no plane exerts more pull here than any other. The closer you walk toward the Spire, the more magic fades. At the base of the Spire, spells stop working entirely. At the Spire's peak: Sigil.

The Outlands is dotted with gate-towns: seventeen settlements each built around a permanent gate to one of the Outer Planes. Each gate-town takes on the character of the plane it leads to — Bedlam runs toward chaos, Excelsior toward righteousness. If a gate-town drifts too far into its plane's alignment, it slides through the gate and becomes part of that plane. A new gate-town grows in its place.

Survival note: The Outlands is the safest neutral transit zone in the multiverse — relatively. Watch which direction you walk. Toward the Spire = less magic. Away from the Spire = into a gate-town, then beyond.

The Outlands — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Mount Celestia
worldLore.body:
Seven layers, each a terrace on an infinite mountain ascending toward perfect good and order. The air here feels clean in a way that makes everything else feel filthy by comparison. Celestials — archons, angels — patrol the terraces. Petitioners climb toward the summit their whole afterlives.

Survival note: You're safe here if your alignment is in the right neighborhood. Evil creatures feel physically ill. The plane's tone pushes you toward self-sacrifice and duty — useful if you need to do something heroic, dangerous if you don't have time for it. Watch for archons who take their job very seriously.

Mount Celestia — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Bytopia
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Neutral Good / Lawful Good
worldLore.body:
Two layers face each other like the inside of a clam shell, with an infinite sky between them. Both layers are pastoral, industrious, fertile. The residents here work hard and like it. Gnomes, halflings, and self-sufficient types feel at home.

Survival note: Friendly plane. No dramatic hazards. The tone nudges you toward honest labor and community — not the worst thing that's happened to a planewalker. Don't expect anyone to do your job for you.

Bytopia — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Elysium
worldLore.body:
The Blessed Fields. Rolling hills, warm light, rivers that flow with calm contentment. The plane radiates peace so strongly that visitors sometimes forget they had anywhere to go. Petitioners here are happy and don't particularly want to leave.

Survival note: The danger in Elysium is that you stop. The plane's tone is overwhelming contentment — the longer you stay, the harder it is to feel urgency about anything. Planewalkers have sat down in a field here "just to rest" and never stood back up. Set a watch. Get out before it feels too good to leave.

Elysium — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: The Beastlands
worldLore.body:
Pure wilderness, three layers of it, cycling through perpetual day, perpetual dusk, and perpetual night. Animals here are intelligent and enormous. The plane is loud, alive, and completely indifferent to civilization. Celestial animals of every kind roam here.

Survival note: You are not at the top of the food chain here. The plane's tone pushes you toward your animal instincts — hunters want to hunt, prey wants to run. Wear your leathers, not your robes. Speak plainly. Druidic types thrive; city folk struggle.

The Beastlands — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Arborea
worldLore.body:
The Olympian Glades. Three layers: endless forest and mountain, a sea that stretches forever, and a third layer of twilight and sorrow. The elven pantheon calls this home. The plane runs hot — joy and grief both peak here. Arborea doesn't do moderation.

Survival note: Beautiful and dangerous. The tone amplifies passion. Emotions run high, decisions get made fast, and violence can erupt from a moment's slight. Elves and bards feel it as inspiration. Everyone else should avoid picking fights. The wine here is very good. Drink carefully.

Arborea — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Ysgard
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Chaotic Neutral / Chaotic Good
worldLore.body:
The Heroic Domains. A plane of floating earthbergs, constant battle, and glorious death. Norse pantheon territory. Warriors here who die in battle wake up the next morning intact, ready to fight again. The plane respects strength and story above everything.

Survival note: You will be challenged, tested, and probably punched. This is fine — it's a compliment. Refusing a challenge marks you as a coward, which is worse than losing. The dead who fight here aren't undead; they're just... doing the thing they love. Don't interrupt. Ysgard respects a good fight more than a living outsider.

Ysgard — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Limbo
worldLore.body:
The Ever-Changing Chaos. No solid ground unless you make it. Limbo is raw matter and energy in constant motion — fire, earth, water, lightning, bone, silk, whatever — swirling together and pulling apart. The githzerai have carved monasteries out of it through sheer willpower. Slaadi (frog-demons of chaos) spawn here in great numbers.

Survival note: You need a strong will to survive Limbo. A trained mind can hold a pocket of stable ground and breathe; a panicking mind gets dissolved. The githzerai can teach you the technique — if you can find one willing to talk. Don't let go of your thoughts. Literally.

Limbo — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Pandemonium
worldLore.body:
The Windswept Depths. Four layers of tunnels cut through infinite dark rock, scoured by winds so loud you can't think. The wind is not natural — it carries voices, whispers, screams of the lost. Petitioners here wander and eventually go mad. The plane is home to the most unhinged of the chaotic evil powers.

Survival note: The wind will deafen you and then break your mind if you stay long enough. Bring earplugs or a silence effect. Navigation is nearly impossible — the tunnels go everywhere and nowhere. Mark your path obsessively. Don't stop moving, and don't listen to what the wind says.

Pandemonium — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: The Abyss
worldLore.body:
Infinite layers, each worse than the last in its own specific way. Home of the tanar'ri (demons). The Blood War — the endless war between demons and devils — is partly fought here. Each layer has its own demon lord, its own logic, its own particular horror. The Abyss wants to corrupt and consume everything that enters it.

Survival note: You should not be here without a plan. The plane's tone is corruption — every hour you spend in the Abyss, it tries to make you a little worse. Don't eat anything. Don't drink anything. Don't make deals. Don't sign anything. The moment you think you understand what's happening, you've already lost something.

The Abyss — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Carceri
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Neutral Evil / Chaotic Evil
worldLore.body:
The Tarterian Depths. Six spheres nested inside each other, each a prison. Carceri traps things — exiles, deposed gods, creatures too dangerous or too broken for anywhere else. The plane itself resists exit. Those who enter expecting to leave find the doors keep moving.

Survival note: The rule about Carceri: it's easy to get in and very hard to get out. The plane actively impedes escape — portals close, paths loop, the terrain conspires. If you're going to Carceri, secure your exit before you step through, not after. Yugoloth mercenaries who work the plane know the exits and will sell that information. For a price.

Carceri — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: The Gray Waste
worldLore.body:
Three layers of gray. Gray sky, gray ground, gray light that drains color from everything, including you. The plane bleeds emotion — visitors slowly lose the ability to feel anything: hope, fear, anger, love. Petitioners here become larvae eventually, worthless husks traded by night hags as currency.

Survival note: The Gray Waste kills you slowly and you won't mind. The emotional drain hits within hours. You'll stop caring about your mission, your companions, your exit. Keep checking yourself against a baseline: remember something that made you angry or glad, and notice if it starts to feel distant. Get out before you can't be bothered.

The Gray Waste of Hades — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Gehenna
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Neutral Evil / Lawful Evil
worldLore.body:
Four layers of volcanic mountain. Steep, erupting, covered in ash. The plane rewards self-interest above all else — cooperation is weakness, trust is a liability. Yugoloths (also called daemons, neutral evil mercenaries) call Gehenna home. They are for hire and will absolutely betray you when it becomes profitable.

Survival note: Don't trust anyone in Gehenna. The tone here makes even decent people start calculating every interaction for personal advantage. Watch your companions. Watch yourself. The yugoloths are the best guides money can buy — they'll get you where you're going as long as it's not worth more to sell you instead. Bid high. They respect that.

Gehenna — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Baator (The Nine Hells)
worldLore.body:
Nine layers, each ruled by an Archdevil. Baator is the most organized evil in the multiverse — hierarchy, contracts, punishment, ambition expressed through bureaucracy. Baatezu (devils) run everything. The Blood War brings demon armies crashing against the first layer, Avernus, constantly. Further down: colder, darker, more controlled.

Survival note: Every contract in Baator is binding. Every word will be used against you. Devils love loopholes and they have had longer to think about them than you have. Get anything in writing — and then assume the writing is also a trap. Baator is the most navigable of the lower planes if you play the game correctly. Most people don't play the game correctly.

Baator (The Nine Hells) — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Acheron
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Lawful Neutral / Lawful Evil
worldLore.body:
The Infinite Battlefield. Four layers of iron cubes, each floating in a void, crashing into each other. Armies have been fighting here since before memory. Goblinoid pantheon territory. The dead soldiers who fought here and lost become the ground — absorbed into the iron and ground down by the next collision.

Survival note: The cubes drift and collide. Two cubes grinding together will kill everything between them. Keep your eyes up. The plane's tone is martial discipline and obedience to the chain of command — you may find yourself following orders you don't remember agreeing to. The armies here will recruit you if they can. Best not to look like you need somewhere to be.

Acheron — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Mechanus
worldLore.body:
Infinite interlocking gears, all turning, all connected, all perfectly timed. The plane embodies law, order, and reason. Modrons — geometric law-beings — maintain everything according to their own inscrutable hierarchy. The gods of order keep their portfolios here.

Survival note: Mechanus rewards patience and precision. The tone pushes you toward order and logic — for most visitors, this just means you stop procrastinating, which is fine. Rules are enforced literally here. Cutting a corner is a physical act with consequences. The modrons will not explain themselves but will report any infraction to the appropriate authority. Follow the rules you can see and assume there are more you can't.

Mechanus — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: Arcadia
worldLore.eyebrow: Outer Planes — Lawful Good / Lawful Neutral
worldLore.body:
The Peaceable Kingdoms. Two layers of perfect order in service of the common good. Crops grow in rows. Villages are clean. Everyone has a purpose and fulfills it. The plane sits between Mechanus and Mount Celestia, and it shows — law and good without the extremes of either.

Survival note: Arcadia is pleasant but expects participation. The tone is civic virtue — you will want to help, contribute, do your share. Crime here is both physically difficult and genuinely unthinkable to most visitors. It's a good place to rest and resupply. Don't cause trouble and Arcadia will treat you well. It's also drifting slightly toward Mechanus, losing some of its good alignment over the centuries. The locals don't like to discuss this.

Arcadia — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

worldLore.title: The Inner Planes
worldLore.body:
The Inner Planes are pure elemental matter: Earth, Air, Fire, Water, and the four para-elemental and quasi-elemental planes between them. The Positive Energy Plane births life; the Negative Energy Plane unmakes it. The Ethereal Plane wraps around all of them.

Most travelers have no business in the Inner Planes unless they're looking for an elemental lord, a rare material, or a very specific kind of trouble. The planes are hostile by nature — the Plane of Fire burns, the Plane of Earth crushes, the Plane of Air has no ground, the Plane of Water has no air. You need magic or native protection to survive more than a few minutes in the wrong element.

Survival note: Know your element before you step through. Protection from Energy doesn't cover everything the plane will do to you. The Ethereal is the transit layer — safer than the elemental planes themselves, used by travelers who know what they're doing. The Astral Plane connects the Outer Planes and is its own kind of hazard: psychic wind, astral dreadnoughts, the silver cords of projecting travelers.

Great Wheel cosmology — Planescape Wiki (Fandom)

gmToolbox.title: Tension Track
gmToolbox.body:
The tension track runs from 0 to 6 and measures how much heat the party has generated in the Hive. It rises through jobs, violence, public scenes, and faction provocation. It does not reset between sessions.

Street appearances by level:

  • T0: Normal Hive street. Peddlers, foot traffic, the usual noise.
  • T1: A Harmonium patrol passes. Nobody stops.
  • T2: Cask or Ninefold muscle watching from a doorway. Not acting yet.
  • T3: Both factions have eyes on the party. Job offers get tested first.
  • T4: Cask and Ninefold soldiers in the same block. Tension is visible.
  • T5: Full street mobilization. Gray Ledger calls in both debts simultaneously.
  • T6: Gang war. Three factions converge. Harmonium arrives with numbers. Tannit Brask (Rusted Bell first) is mazed. Cask second and Ninefold second are mazed. The Lady of Pain has made her move.

Payoff reduction: At T0-3, job rewards pay at 1/3. At T4-5, rewards pay at 1/2. At T6, the arc ends regardless of quest state — the Gray Ledger reveal is forced.

Rusted Bell revenge thread: After Tannit Brask is mazed at T6, a new first takes over and sends a letter to the party. This thread carries forward into Arc 2.

gmToolbox.title: Portal and Haven Rules
gmToolbox.body:
Portals in Sigil require a key — a specific object, word, action, or condition. No key, no transit. The portal simply does not activate.

New Haven haven rule — 4 conditions required:

  1. A roof over one's head
  2. A host who has invited you in
  3. A meal shared at the table
  4. A welcome spoken aloud

All four must be present. Missing any one condition means the portal to New Haven does not open from that location.

Horus exception: The party is Horus's household. They are considered permanent hosts of his house. When one party member cooks using food already in the house, conditions 1-3 are automatically satisfied. They still must speak the welcome aloud.

Sand Globe: Once per week, the globe can send up to 8 creatures to New Haven for up to 12 hours. Bypasses the four-condition check entirely.

Ethereal Anchor Box: Things trickle through the Ethereal into the box passively. Closing the portal stops new arrivals but does not eject what is already inside. Retrieving an object: DC 20 (known object) or DC 25 (unknown). The New Haven spirit flood is a known risk if the box is left open too long near an active Ethereal current.

gmToolbox.title: Planescape Calendar
gmToolbox.body:
The planar calendar runs 13 months of exactly 28 days each, totaling 364 days per year. There are no leap years. Months are named for philosophical and planar concepts rather than seasons.

Current date: 21st of Nihilum, Year 141.

Month list: Mortis, Ignis, Aether, Causus, Liminus, Ordinis, Caelum, Obscurum, Nexum, Vitalis, Nihilum, Arcanum, Terminus.

Nihilum (month 11) is associated with endings and transitions — traditionally when debts come due and contracts expire. The party's arc begins here deliberately.

Full calendar available at Fantasy Calendar.

gmToolbox.title: S.I.G.I.S. Ad Intel
gmToolbox.body:
Two active ad frameworks with mechanical hooks.

ad23 — Soul Enforcement (Pollus Windscream): A soul-broker named Pollus Windscream is advertising for stag-turners — people willing to track down an escaped Baator soul. The soul got out through a contract loophole. Pollus is not evil; he is a bureaucrat with a filing problem. The party is handed a bare moral choice with no obvious correct answer and no twist. The ad is framed only; the job resolves however the party decides.

ad14 — Dead God Ritual (Grax at the Red Lantern): A tiefling named Grax is running a job out of the Red Lantern tavern in the Lower Ward. Githyanki have identified the site of a dead god's last resting place and are performing a ritual extraction. The job is to disrupt or redirect the ritual. Heat tracker: combat only — every hit landed and every kill adds heat; if heat maxes out before the ritual is disrupted, the session enters a survival sequence instead of a success state. The tick-down action (what stops the ritual short of combat) is still open design.
